slides.say: Data Science from Scratch, lesson eleven: choosing the right chart.
Start with the question, not the chart. Are you comparing groups, showing a trend over time, showing a distribution, or showing a relationship between two things?

To compare categories, use a bar chart, like the number of transactions by payment method. It's usually easier to read than a pie chart, especially with many slices. And start the bars at zero, so differences aren't exaggerated.
To show a trend over time, use a line chart, like monthly loan applications. Time usually goes along the horizontal axis, from left to right.

slides.sub: How transaction amounts are spread out
slides.say: To show a distribution, use a histogram or a box plot. They show where most values sit, how spread out they are, and whether there are outliers.

slides.sub: Income vs loan amount · one dot per customer
slides.say: To show the relationship between two number columns, use a scatter plot, like income against loan amount. Each dot is one customer.

slides.text: Question first, then pick the chart.
slides.say: So the takeaway: decide the question first, then pick the simplest chart that answers it.

summary: Choose a chart by the question you are answering: bar charts compare categories, line charts show trends over time, histograms and box plots show distributions, and scatter plots show the relationship between two numeric columns.
practice: Write four questions about your own spending, for example 'Which category do I spend most on?' or 'Is my spending rising month by month?'. For each one, name the chart you would use (bar, line, histogram or scatter) and sketch it on paper.
